en: Mount Pinatubo stayed quiet for a very long time, then in 1991 produced one of the largest eruptions of the last hundred years.
Philippine volcanoes sit on the Ring of Fire, where one plate dives under another, so magma keeps rising and eruptions keep happening.
Most Philippine eruptions in the last hundred years have been smaller than Pinatubo in 1991, so giant blasts are rare in the record.
After an eruption, heavy rain can turn loose ash into lahars for years, a repeating hazard that follows many Philippine blasts.
Pinatubo's 1991 eruption showed a long-quiet volcano can still hold a very large blast after a long rest.
The 1991 Pinatubo eruption sent so much ash and gas high into the air that it briefly cooled climate around the world.
Taal's 2020 eruption sent ash across nearby provinces, a sudden event after years of quieter steaming in the lake.
Many Philippine volcanoes have thick, sticky magma, so they more often blast ash and rocks than pour out very runny lava.
A fair test changes only one thing at a time so you can tell which change caused the new result.
When you measure water in a cylinder, read the bottom of the curve at eye level so every trial uses the same reading habit.
When a sounding object moves away from you, its sound waves stretch out, so you hear a lower pitch than before.
Behind a moving sound source the wavelength is longer, so a listener there hears a lower frequency.
Whenever the gap between a sound and your ear is opening quickly, fewer waves arrive each second and the pitch tends to fall.
A famous difference: S-waves do not travel through Earth's liquid outer core, while P-waves do, which helped map that liquid layer.
In a guided activity, talk into a tight-string cup phone and let your partner listen, so you feel how sound can carry a message along the string.
Alert Level 0 means the volcano is quiet, with no extra unrest, so daily life can go on while PHIVOLCS still keeps watching.
Alert Level 4 means a hazardous eruption is possible within days, so people in mapped danger zones should leave before the blast, not after it starts.
Green plants use sunlight to make food in photosynthesis, so almost every lunch on Earth traces back to energy from the Sun.
A falling object feels gravity pulling down and air pushing up, so a fair prediction asks which of those two forces matters more this time.
Gravity makes a falling object go faster the longer it falls, and that speeding up is about the same for compact heavy and light objects.
A light, wide object can reach a steady falling speed when air push equals weight, so it stops speeding up while a rock still does.
A parachute is made wide so air resistance becomes large on purpose; that is why a person with a parachute falls more slowly than a dropped bag of rice.
A PAGASA Public Storm Warning Signal is a number that matches how strong the winds are expected to be in a named place.
Signal Number 1 means strong winds of about 39 to 61 kilometers per hour are expected, enough to snap twigs and make sea travel rough for small boats.
Signal Number 2 means gale-force winds of about 62 to 88 kilometers per hour, which can break small branches and bother light houses.
Signal Number 3 means stormy winds of about 89 to 117 kilometers per hour, with heavy rain likely and a real risk of damage to many roofs.
Signal Number 4 means typhoon-force winds of about 118 to 184 kilometers per hour, weather that can heavily damage houses and knock down many trees.
Signal Number 5 means winds of about 185 kilometers per hour or more, weather that can cause widespread, catastrophic damage where the signal is raised.
PAGASA can raise or lower a signal as the cyclone's path and strength change, so the expected weather for your town can change in a later bulletin.
Very loud sound can hurt the ears, so stepping away from a screaming speaker is a way to protect your hearing.
Do not look straight at the Sun to 'check' an eclipse; that light can harm eyes, so use a safe projector or stay with an adult's method.
Bright sunlight bouncing off water or sand can still hurt eyes, so a hat brim and looking away are protections at the beach too.
Earth's yearly path around the Sun changes which constellations show at night, so the year itself could be checked against the sky.
In the north, Polaris sits almost still while other stars wheel around it, so it was a trusted marker for the direction north.
Air is a mixture of gases, mainly nitrogen and oxygen, plus smaller amounts of carbon dioxide, water vapor, and other gases.
